countries.name: Brunei
countries.summary: Brunei is hot and humid all year, with rain falling every month. February to April is the driest period, and the northeast monsoon makes November to January the wettest. countries.name: China
countries.summary: China spans subarctic Harbin, tropical Hainan, the Tibetan plateau and the Taklamakan desert. Spring (April–May) and autumn (September–October) are the best times for most of the country. Summer is hot, humid and wet across the monsoon-fed east and south, while winters in the north are bitterly cold and dry. Avoid the three national holiday weeks: Chinese New Year (January/February), Labour Day (May 1–5) and Golden Week (October 1–7), when hundreds of millions travel and sights are overwhelmed.

countries.name: Japan
countries.summary: Japan's four seasons are sharply defined. Cherry blossom (late March to early April) and the autumn leaves (mid-to-late November) are the classic peaks. June to mid-July brings the tsuyu rainy season everywhere except Hokkaido. July and August are hot and sticky, and typhoons are most likely from August to September. Winter is dry and sunny on the Pacific side, while the Sea of Japan coast and Hokkaido get some of the deepest powder snow on earth. Golden Week, Obon and New Year are the big domestic travel peaks.

regions.name: Honshu, Shikoku & Kyushu
regions.description: Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka, Nara, Hiroshima, Hakone and Mt Fuji, the Japanese Alps, Kanazawa, Shikoku and Kyushu (Fukuoka, Nagasaki).

best.why: Cherry-blossom season: hanami picnics under the sakura in Tokyo and Kyoto, mild 15–20 °C days.
After Golden Week: warm, green and noticeably quieter, with azaleas and the Alps opening up.
Crisp, clear autumn: fiery momiji leaves in Kyoto, Nikko and Hakone, with good views of Mt Fuji.

worst.why: Hot and humid (32–36 °C) with heatstroke warnings, Obon crowds in mid-August and the typhoon risk rising.

shoulder.why: Spring continues, but Golden Week (Apr 29 – May 5) brings domestic crowds and higher prices.
Tsuyu rainy season: grey and humid, but hydrangeas bloom and there are few tourists. Mt Fuji's climbing season opens July 10.
Still warm, with September the typhoon peak; autumn leaves haven't turned yet.
Cold but dry and sunny on the Pacific side with winter illuminations; ski season in the Alps and the cheapest hotels outside New Year.

risks.note: Typhoons can halt Shinkansen and flights for a day or two; September is the peak.
Heatstroke alerts are common; plan indoor breaks at midday.
Rainy-season downpours can trigger landslides in mountain areas.

regions.name: Hokkaido

shoulder.why: Ski season opens; New Year is a busy peak.

countries.name: Laos
countries.summary: Laos is landlocked and laid-back, with three seasons: cool and dry (November–February), hot and hazy (March–April) and green and rainy (May–October). The cool season is best for Luang Prabang, the Mekong slow boat and trekking. In the late dry season, smoke from field burning hides the mountains.
countries.splitReason: Laos follows one monsoon calendar: dry from November to April and wet from May to October. The northern hills are cooler (and hazy in March–April) but share the same seasons.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: The whole country: Luang Prabang, Vientiane, Vang Vieng, Nong Khiaw, the Bolaven Plateau and the 4,000 Islands.

best.why: Cool, dry season: misty mornings in Luang Prabang, Mekong slow boats and turquoise water at the Kuang Si falls.

worst.why: Slash-and-burn haze hides the mountains, with 35 °C heat.

shoulder.why: Warming, with haze starting.
Pi Mai Lao (New Year) water festival in mid-April.

prices.notes: Very affordable. The Laos–China railway makes Vientiane–Vang Vieng–Luang Prabang fast; book tickets early.

countries.name: Malaysia
countries.summary: Malaysia is hot and humid all year (30–33 °C), but its monsoons hit different coasts at different times. The west coast (Penang, Langkawi, KL) is best from December to March and wettest in October–November. The east-coast islands (Perhentian, Redang, Tioman) are only open from about March to October, closing for the northeast monsoon. Malaysian Borneo (Sabah, Sarawak) is driest from February to April and great for diving and wildlife most of the year.

regions.description: Kuala Lumpur, Penang (George Town), Langkawi, Malacca, Ipoh, the Cameron Highlands and Taman Negara.

best.why: The west coast's driest, sunniest spell: calm seas around Langkawi and Penang and pleasant city strolls.

worst.why: Inter-monsoon season brings the heaviest thunderstorms, and Langkawi's sea gets choppy.

countries.name: Mongolia
countries.summary: Mongolia is the land of blue sky, with over 250 sunny days a year but brutal cold. Ulaanbaatar is the world's coldest capital (−25 °C in January). The travel window is short: June to mid-September brings green steppe, open ger camps and the Naadam festival in July. Late September and October give golden larch forests and the Golden Eagle Festival, with freezing nights.
countries.splitReason: Mongolia's extreme continental climate gives the whole country one short travel season, June to September. The Gobi is hotter and drier and the north greener, but both peak at the same time.

regions.name: Whole country

countries.name: Myanmar
countries.summary: Myanmar's best season is the cool, dry winter (November–February), when hot-air balloons drift over Bagan's temples. It becomes extremely hot from March to May, and the monsoon (June–October) soaks Yangon and the coast. Since the 2021 coup and the ongoing conflict, many governments advise against travel to much of the country, so check current advice before planning.

Climatically it mirrors northern Korea: cold, dry winters, a wet July–August monsoon, and clear springs and autumns, which are the times tours run most.

countries.name: Philippines
countries.summary: The Philippines has 7,600 islands and a dry season that runs roughly from December to May across the west and centre (Manila, Palawan, Boracay, Cebu). Typhoons can strike from June to December, peaking from August to November, and the Visayas and northern Luzon take the most hits. The Pacific-facing east (Siargao) runs the other way: it's wettest from November to February under the northeast monsoon and driest from April to October.

countries.name: Singapore
countries.summary: Singapore is hot and humid all year (31–32 °C), and short, heavy thunderstorms can happen any day. February to April is the driest and sunniest period. November to January is wettest with the northeast monsoon. Smoke haze from Indonesian fires sometimes arrives from August to October. The F1 night race (around late September) and Chinese New Year push hotel prices up.

countries.name: South Korea

countries.name: Sri Lanka

Hot and getting humid, with inter-monsoon showers building.

risks.note: Northeast monsoon; roads to Arugam Bay can flood.
Bay of Bengal cyclones occasionally make landfall on the east coast.

recurringHolidays.name: Kataragama Esala festival
recurringHolidays.approx: July/August, about 2 weeks before the Esala full moon
recurringHolidays.effect: Pilgrim crowds near Arugam Bay and the Kumana area; buses full.

recurringHolidays.name: Sinhala & Tamil New Year
recurringHolidays.effect: Closures and packed transport.

recurringHolidays.name: Sri Lankan school holidays
recurringHolidays.effect: Domestic tourists fill Trincomalee and Pasikudah hotels.

prices.notes: Cheaper than the south-west. Pasikudah's big resorts discount heavily outside May–September.

regions.name: Hill Country
regions.description: Kandy, Nuwara Eliya, Hatton and Adam's Peak, Ella, Haputale, Horton Plains and the tea estates of the central highlands.

best.why: The driest spell across the highlands: clear views from the Kandy–Ella train, sunrise on Adam's Peak during pilgrimage season (Dec–May) and tea country at its best.

worst.why: Rain on both sides of the hills (inter-monsoon plus northeast monsoon): misty viewpoints, leeches on trails and a high risk of landslides.

shoulder.why: 'April season' in Nuwara Eliya: festive but busy, with prices doubling. Showers increase.
The southwest monsoon soaks the western slopes (Hatton, Nuwara Eliya), while Ella and Haputale are drier.
A mixed picture: often dry on the eastern side (Ella). The Kandy Esala Perahera procession is the cultural highlight of the year.
Showers return across the hills, but it's quiet and cheap.
Rains easing; Adam's Peak pilgrimage season begins on the December Poya.

risks.note: Western slopes during the southwest monsoon.
The highest risk across the hills; roads and the railway are occasionally cut.

recurringHolidays.name: Kandy Esala Perahera
recurringHolidays.approx: July/August, 10 nights before the Esala full moon
recurringHolidays.effect: Nightly processions with elephants. Kandy rooms triple in price and sell out months ahead.

recurringHolidays.name: Nuwara Eliya 'April season'
recurringHolidays.effect: Horse races and festivities; hotel prices double.

recurringHolidays.name: Adam's Peak pilgrimage season
recurringHolidays.effect: Weekend and Poya nights see thousands of climbers on the trail; go midweek.

recurringHolidays.name: Sinhala & Tamil New Year
recurringHolidays.effect: Trains booked out and many businesses closed.

prices.notes: Reserved seats on the Kandy–Ella train sell out weeks ahead in peak season. Tea-estate bungalows are a splurge worth booking early.

regions.name: Cultural Triangle & North
regions.description: Sigiriya, Dambulla, Polonnaruwa, Anuradhapura, Habarana, Minneriya and Kaudulla parks, plus Jaffna and the north.

best.why: Dry, with clear mornings for climbing Sigiriya and cycling around the Polonnaruwa ruins. The northeast monsoon has ended.
Mostly dry and breezy. The Minneriya elephant 'Gathering' (Jul–Sep) is one of Asia's great wildlife spectacles.

worst.why: The heaviest rains of the year (inter-monsoon plus northeast monsoon) flood the plains around Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa.

shoulder.why: Rains easing; Christmas brings busy hotels.
Hot (34 °C) and humid. Vesak lanterns light up the temples in May.
Hot, with storms building; the elephant gathering winds down.

risks.note: Climb Sigiriya at opening time (7 am) to avoid the 34 °C midday heat.
Monsoon flooding on the dry-zone plains; reservoirs overflow.

recurringHolidays.name: Vesak Poya
recurringHolidays.effect: Huge pilgrim numbers at Anuradhapura and Dambulla; lantern festivals.

recurringHolidays.name: Poson Poya
recurringHolidays.effect: Hundreds of thousands of pilgrims at Anuradhapura and Mihintale; roads jammed.

recurringHolidays.name: Sinhala & Tamil New Year
recurringHolidays.effect: Closures and packed transport.

prices.notes: Site tickets are a big part of the budget: Sigiriya costs about $36 and the Polonnaruwa and Anuradhapura combined tickets about $25 each.

countries.name: Taiwan
countries.summary: Taiwan is subtropical in the north and tropical in the south. The north and east coast get a damp, drizzly northeast monsoon in winter, while the south stays dry and sunny. Everywhere has plum rains in May–June and typhoons from July to September, which can close the mountain roads through Taroko Gorge and to Alishan. Autumn (October–November) and spring (March–April) are the most reliable.

regions.name: North & East Coast
regions.description: Taipei, Jiufen, Yilan, the east coast (Hualien, Taroko Gorge, Taitung) and the northern mountains.

best.why: Drier and 20–26 °C: comfortable hiking in Taroko and Yangmingshan.
Spring blossoms and warm days before the plum rains.

worst.why: Typhoon season: Taroko Gorge roads close, with heavy rain and very humid heat.

shoulder.why: Cool (13–20 °C), damp and drizzly from the northeast monsoon in Taipei and Keelung, plus Lunar New Year closures.
Plum rains, then hot, humid summer.
Typhoon risk is fading.

risks.note: Typhoons close schools and offices and cut mountain roads.
Plum-rain downpours.
The Taroko and Central Cross-Island roads are vulnerable.

recurringHolidays.effect: Week-long holiday: trains sold out and many restaurants close.

recurringHolidays.name: Tomb Sweeping Day
recurringHolidays.effect: Long weekend; heavy domestic travel.

recurringHolidays.name: Double Ten (National Day)
recurringHolidays.effect: Long-weekend crowds and fireworks.

prices.notes: Taipei is good value for food. Taroko Gorge is best done from Hualien by scooter or tour.

regions.name: Centre & South
regions.description: Taichung, Sun Moon Lake, Alishan, Tainan, Kaohsiung, Kenting, Penghu and Green Island.

best.why: Dry season: sunny 24–28 °C winters, and Kenting's beaches are swimmable most of the year.

worst.why: The southwest monsoon and typhoons bring the heaviest rain, with afternoon deluges.

shoulder.why: Hot, with the plum rains starting in mid-May.
Rains easing, with sunnier and calmer days.

risks.note: Direct hits on the south and east.
Southwest-monsoon deluges.

recurringHolidays.name: Lunar New Year

recurringHolidays.effect: Week-long holiday: trains sold out and many restaurants close.

recurringHolidays.effect: Long weekend; heavy domestic travel.

recurringHolidays.name: Double Ten (National Day)
recurringHolidays.effect: Long-weekend crowds and fireworks.

countries.name: Thailand
countries.summary: Thailand has three seasons: cool and dry (November–February), hot (March–May) and the rainy monsoon (roughly May–October). The two coasts run on opposite calendars. The Andaman side (Phuket, Krabi) is at its best from December to March and rough in the southwest monsoon. The Gulf islands (Koh Samui, Phangan, Tao) stay fairly dry through the European summer but take a drenching in October–December. The north adds a 'burning season' of smoky haze in March–April.

regions.name: Northern Thailand
regions.description: Chiang Mai, Chiang Rai, Pai, the Mae Hong Son loop, Sukhothai and the northern mountains.

best.why: The cool dry season brings 28–30 °C days and 14–18 °C nights, clear mountain views and comfortable trekking. The Yi Peng lantern festival lights up Chiang Mai in November.

worst.why: Burning season: crop-burning smoke makes Chiang Mai's air among the most polluted in the world, hides the mountain views and comes with 36 °C heat.
The wettest months bring muddy, leech-heavy treks and landslides on mountain roads such as the Mae Hong Son loop.

shoulder.why: Warming up and still mostly clear, but haze can start in late February.
Songkran (Apr 13–15) is famously wild in Chiang Mai, but it's very hot and the haze lingers.
Green season: lush paddies, short afternoon storms and low prices.
Rains ease off and the landscape is at its greenest, just before peak prices.

risks.note: Crop-burning haze. Check the AQI daily; people with asthma should avoid this period.
Afternoon heat of 36–40 °C before the rains arrive.
Southwest monsoon: daily storms that are heaviest in August and September.
Mountain roads around Pai and Mae Hong Son can be cut off.

recurringHolidays.name: Songkran (Thai New Year)
recurringHolidays.effect: Nationwide water fights, with Chiang Mai the epicentre: buses and hotels book out and many businesses close.

recurringHolidays.name: Chinese New Year
recurringHolidays.approx: Late Jan / Feb, moves each year
recurringHolidays.effect: A surge of regional visitors: hotels fill and prices rise.

recurringHolidays.name: Yi Peng & Loy Krathong
recurringHolidays.effect: Chiang Mai's lantern festival: rooms triple in price and sell out months ahead.

recurringHolidays.name: Christmas & New Year
recurringHolidays.effect: Peak-season prices and minimum stays.

prices.notes: Pai and Chiang Mai guesthouses double in price around Yi Peng. Treks and elephant-sanctuary visits cost about the same all year.

regions.name: Bangkok & Central Thailand
regions.description: Bangkok, Ayutthaya, Kanchanaburi, Khao Yai, plus the upper Gulf resorts of Hua Hin and Pattaya.

best.why: The driest and least humid time: about 31 °C days, clear skies for temples, river trips and night markets, and comfortable evenings.

worst.why: The hottest time of year, with a heat index of 40–45 °C and nights that barely cool. Sightseeing is draining (Songkran week is fun but chaotic).
The peak of the rains brings daily downpours and flash flooding in Bangkok's streets and sois, with heavy traffic.

shoulder.why: Dry but heating up quickly (34–35 °C).
Green season: short heavy showers, mostly dry mornings and good hotel deals.
Rains easing; the Loy Krathong river festival in November.

risks.note: Heat index often 42 °C or more in the afternoons; plan indoor breaks.
Urban flash flooding after storms; Chao Phraya river flooding in very wet years.
PM2.5 smog episodes in Bangkok during the dry season.

recurringHolidays.name: Songkran (Thai New Year)
recurringHolidays.effect: Water fights on Khao San and Silom Roads; many Bangkokians leave the city, so long-distance transport is full.

recurringHolidays.name: Chinese New Year in Yaowarat
recurringHolidays.approx: Late Jan / Feb, moves each year
recurringHolidays.effect: Chinatown celebrations; hotel demand rises.

recurringHolidays.name: Loy Krathong
recurringHolidays.effect: Candle floats on the river; riverside hotels book up.

recurringHolidays.name: Christmas & New Year
recurringHolidays.effect: Peak rates in Bangkok, Hua Hin and Pattaya.

prices.notes: Bangkok has a huge hotel supply, so prices vary less by season than at the beaches. Hua Hin weekends fill with Bangkok residents.

regions.name: Andaman Coast
regions.description: The west coast and islands on the Andaman Sea: Phuket, Krabi and Ao Nang, Koh Phi Phi, Koh Lanta, Khao Lak, the Similan and Surin islands, and Koh Lipe.

best.why: The dry northeast monsoon brings calm, clear turquoise water, reliable sunshine and the best diving visibility. The Similan and Surin marine parks are open, and island-hopping boats run daily.

worst.why: The southwest monsoon brings rough seas and red-flag beaches with deadly rip currents. The Similan and Surin parks close, many island ferries stop and rain falls most days.

shoulder.why: Hot (33 °C) and still calm, with fewer people. Songkran falls mid-month.
The monsoon arrives in the second half of the month, with the last dive trips before the parks close.
Rains taper off and the marine parks reopen around Oct 15. It's still showery, but prices are low.

risks.note: Southwest monsoon: heavy squalls, with September the wettest month.
Rip currents cause drownings every year; obey the red flags. Many speedboat routes are suspended.

recurringHolidays.name: Christmas & New Year
recurringHolidays.effect: Peak rates (2–3× low season) with minimum stays; book months ahead.

recurringHolidays.name: Chinese New Year
recurringHolidays.approx: Late Jan / Feb, moves each year
recurringHolidays.effect: Phuket and Krabi fill with regional visitors.

recurringHolidays.name: Songkran
recurringHolidays.effect: Water festival in Patong and Phuket Town.

recurringHolidays.name: Phuket Vegetarian Festival
recurringHolidays.effect: Spectacular processions in Phuket Town; local hotels busy.

prices.notes: Low-season discounts of 40–60% on resorts are common. Phi Phi and Koh Lipe are the most expensive islands in peak season.

regions.name: Gulf Islands (Samui, Phangan, Tao)
regions.description: Koh Samui, Koh Phangan, Koh Tao and Ang Thong Marine Park in the southern Gulf of Thailand.

best.why: The driest, calmest months: glassy sea, excellent snorkelling at Koh Tao and Ang Thong, and day after day of sunshine.
Mostly dry, with only brief showers, while the Andaman coast is in monsoon. This is Thailand's best beach option in the European summer.

worst.why: The northeast monsoon hits the Gulf: November is the wettest month (500 mm or more), with flooding, cancelled ferries and murky diving.

shoulder.why: The monsoon tails off with mixed days, but holiday prices are at their highest.
Hot, with short showers and quieter beaches.
Showers increase towards October, but there are still plenty of sunny spells and deals.

risks.note: Northeast monsoon; flooding on Samui's ring road in heavy years.
Ferries between Samui, Phangan and Tao are often cancelled and diving is poor.

recurringHolidays.approx: Monthly, on or near the full moon
recurringHolidays.effect: Haad Rin rooms sell out and ferry prices rise for 3–4 nights each month.

recurringHolidays.effect: Peak prices despite mixed weather.

recurringHolidays.name: Chinese New Year
recurringHolidays.approx: Late Jan / Feb, moves each year
recurringHolidays.effect: Busy, with higher rates on Samui.

recurringHolidays.name: Songkran
recurringHolidays.effect: Water festival on Chaweng and Lamai beach roads.

prices.notes: Koh Tao is one of the world's cheapest places to get dive-certified. Samui flights (Bangkok Airways) are pricey, so the ferry via Surat Thani is the budget route.

countries.name: Timor-Leste
countries.summary: Timor-Leste is one of Asia's least-visited countries, with pristine reefs at Atauro Island, whale migrations (October–November) and mountain villages. The dry season (May–November) is the time to go. December to March brings heavy rain that cuts off mountain roads.
countries.splitReason: Timor-Leste is a small, mountainous half-island with one monsoon pattern.

regions.name: Whole country
regions.description: The whole country: Dili, Atauro Island, Mt Ramelau, Baucau and Jaco Island.

best.why: Dry season: whale migration off Dili (October–November), superb diving at Atauro and passable roads up Mt Ramelau.

worst.why: Wet season: landslides close the mountain roads.

shoulder.why: Rains are tailing off.
The rains are arriving.

risks.note: Mountain roads are often cut.

prices.notes: Uses the US dollar. There's little tourist infrastructure, so expect simple guesthouses.

countries.name: Vietnam
countries.summary: Vietnam stretches 1,650 km north to south, so its three regions follow different calendars. The north (Hanoi, Ha Long Bay, Sapa) has a cool, drizzly winter and a hot, wet summer. The centre (Hue, Hoi An, Da Nang) is dry and hot from February to August but gets the country's heaviest rain and typhoons from October to November. The south (Saigon, the Mekong, Phu Quoc) is tropical, with a dry season from December to April. So somewhere is always good, but no single month is perfect everywhere.

regions.name: North Vietnam
regions.description: Hanoi, Ha Long and Lan Ha bays, Ninh Binh, Sapa and the Ha Giang loop.

best.why: Dry and sunny at 20–28 °C: clear views over Ha Long Bay, golden rice terraces around Sapa, and the Ha Giang loop at its best.
Spring warmth and blooming countryside before the rains.

worst.why: Hot (33 °C) and humid with heavy rain; Gulf of Tonkin typhoons can cancel Ha Long cruises.

shoulder.why: Cool and grey with crachin drizzle (14–20 °C); Sapa can freeze; Tết closures.
Hot, with storms building.
Sapa's harvest gold, but typhoons are possible.

risks.note: Ha Long cruises are suspended when storm warnings are issued.
Flash floods and landslides in the northern mountains.
Hanoi has smoggy winter days.

regions.description: Hue, Hoi An, Da Nang, Phong Nha caves, Quy Nhon and Nha Trang.

best.why: Dry and sunny without the summer heat: beach days at My Khe and An Bang, calm sea and lantern-lit nights in Hoi An.

worst.why: Typhoons and Vietnam's heaviest rains: Hoi An's old town floods and the sea is rough.

shoulder.why: Hot (34–38 °C) and busy with Vietnamese holidaymakers, but dry with a calm sea.
Rains begin and typhoons become possible.
Cool, cloudy and drizzly, with Tết in late January or February.

Hoi An's old town and Hue flood most years.
Dry 'Laos winds' push temperatures to 38 °C.

worst.why: Peak southwest monsoon: rough sea and heavy rain on Phu Quoc, and the Mekong floods begin.
